title: tsgolint Reaches Stable v7, Bringing Go-Powered Type-Aware Linting to Oxlint
gist: tsgolint v7 gives VoidZero's Rust-based Oxlint type-aware TypeScript linting that is 12-18x faster than ESLint with typescript-eslint by embedding typescript-go rather than reimplementing a type checker, covering 59 of 61 type-aware rules — a strategic bet that inheriting the official compiler beats Biome's approach of synthesising its own types, which catches only ~75% of cases on one rule.

insights.claim: Benchmarks on microsoft/vscode, microsoft/typescript, typeorm and vuejs/core on an Apple M4 Pro put the stable tsgolint build at 12 to 18 times faster than ESLint with typescript-eslint.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: An order-of-magnitude CI time reduction on the slowest static-analysis tier is a direct compute-cost saving for large TypeScript shops.
insights.locator: The team's benchmarks put the stable build

insights.claim: The release tracks TypeScript v7.0.2 and covers 59 of typescript-eslint's 61 type-aware rules, up from 43 at the December alpha.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Near-complete rule parity removes the last functional reason to stay on ESLint for type-aware linting.

insights.claim: Type-aware linting is the most expensive tier of static analysis because it requires a real model of a program's types to answer questions a single file cannot, such as whether a promise is ever awaited.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Explains why this specific tier was the last to be rewritten in native code and where the remaining CI time sits.
insights.locator: Linting is the static-analysis step that flags likely bugs

themes.theme: Architecture: embed the compiler, don't reimplement it

insights.claim: Rather than reimplementing a type checker, tsgolint builds real TypeScript programs on top of typescript-go, the official Go port of the compiler that ships as TypeScript 7.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Reusing the official compiler shifts maintenance burden onto Microsoft and guarantees semantic fidelity — a durable structural advantage.
insights.locator: tsgolint handles the rules that need TypeScript semantic analysis

insights.claim: Oxlint, written in Rust, handles file discovery, configuration and cheap syntactic rules, then passes the type-aware work to a Go binary that returns structured diagnostics — a deliberate two-language split.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Polyglot tool architecture is becoming acceptable where each language wins a layer — a template other toolchains may copy.
insights.locator: Oxlint, written in Rust, handles file discovery

insights.claim: Writing before the release, Jökull Sólberg concluded Oxlint is making the right long-term bet because aligning with tsgo inherits every future optimisation the TypeScript team ships while keeping the rule surface identical to typescript-eslint.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Free-riding on upstream compiler optimisation is the core strategic argument — the compounding advantage accrues without Oxlint spending.
insights.quote: Oxlint is making the right long-term bet
insights.locator: Writing before the release, Jökull Sólberg concluded

insights.claim: The jump straight from the experimental 0.x line to stable v7 is deliberate, because tsgolint is now versioned against the compiler it embeds, with v7.0.2000 aligning with TypeScript 7.0.2.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Version coupling to the compiler signals the project's dependency and release cadence is now set by Microsoft's.
insights.locator: The jump straight from the experimental 0.x line

themes.theme: Competitive position against Biome and typescript-eslint

insights.claim: Biome v2 synthesises its own types without the compiler, and one analysis puts its noFloatingPromises rule at roughly 75 percent of the cases typescript-eslint catches — a gap Vite creator Evan You has publicly questioned.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Quantifies the correctness cost of reimplementing type inference — the concrete argument against Biome's architecture.
insights.locator: The same argument runs through a Biome discussion

insights.claim: The typescript-eslint team, whose contributor auvred created the original tsgolint prototype, still calls its own tsgolint fork an experiment that is not under active development.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The incumbent ceding the fast path to a competitor that productised its own prototype is a notable ecosystem hand-off.
insights.locator: The typescript-eslint team, whose contributor auvred

insights.claim: On the oxc side correctness is still being refined, with users filing reports such as one where an autofix removed a type assertion that tsc actually required.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Autofix bugs that break compilation are a real adoption risk that offsets the speed argument in the near term.
insights.locator: On the oxc side, correctness is still being refined

insights.claim: Oxlint is part of oxc, a suite of Rust-based JavaScript tools developed under VoidZero, the company Evan You founded to consolidate a famously fragmented toolchain, and its stable release lands amid a wider rewrite of that toolchain in native languages from bundlers and formatters to the TypeScript compiler itself.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: VoidZero is consolidating a fragmented toolchain into one vendor-controlled stack — the key thing to track for JavaScript tooling economics.
insights.locator: Oxlint is the linter in oxc

insights.claim: Adoption takes two commands — installing oxlint and oxlint-tsgolint@7, then running oxlint with --type-aware — with --type-check reporting compiler errors alongside lint diagnostics from the same TypeScript program.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Reusing one TypeScript program for both compile errors and lint diagnostics collapses two CI steps into one.

insights.claim: ESLint users can translate an existing config with npx @oxlint/migrate --type-aware, but the catch is the dependency: type-aware linting requires TypeScript 7.0 or later, some legacy tsconfig options such as baseUrl are unsupported, and projects using removed TypeScript 6 features must migrate first.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The real adoption gate is a TypeScript 7 upgrade, not the linter swap — a much larger migration than the headline suggests.

insights.claim: The release adds per-rule timings surfaced with oxlint --type-aware --debug timings, letting teams see which type-aware rules dominate a run.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Per-rule cost visibility lets teams trade specific rules against CI budget — a practical lever once linting is fast.
insights.locator: The release also adds per-rule timings

insights.claim: Remaining work focuses on the final rules, editor integration and monorepo performance, indicating large-repository workflows are not yet fully covered.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Monorepo performance is exactly where the biggest enterprise users live — adoption there is still pending.
insights.locator: Work now focuses on the final rules
